headToHead.voiceVerdict: Cover the names and Liam is identifiable by shape alone: formal clauses applied to something trivial, then an exclamatory plea or a self-defeating flourish ('So disruptive!', 'Someone stop this madness!'). Dash is identifiable only by vocabulary (churn, pivot, conversion, roadmap). Strip the jargon and his shape is Claim. Fragment. Deflating fragment., which is the same clipped deadpan Frost, Vex and Tilly use. Only the Rooftop line has a shape that belongs to him: a live mid-clause pivot. Bar wins.
headToHead.constructionVerdict: Ours is tighter and ends on the punch word more reliably ('lawsuits', 'ghosts', 'engaged', 'passwords'). The bar is looser (the time-machine line has no turn on its own), but every Liam turn comes from Liam being wrong without noticing (360 degrees), while Dash's turns come from Dash noticing and confessing. Economy goes to ours and depth of turn to the bar, so it is a tie.
headToHead.quotableVerdict: 'Your click rate is lawsuits', 'your entire demographic is ghosts' and 'profitable or engaged' would clip. But 'Save me from the consequences of my actions!' and the 360-degree spin are lines people actually repeat, because the character's self-image is the joke. No Dash line is a character portrait in one sentence the way those are. Bar wins narrowly.

ruleBreaks: No line over its word limit (112 lines checked: openers 12, jabs 10, three-words exactly 3, everything else 20). No em dashes, no emoji, no brands or real people, nothing past PG-13, no 'as an AI'.

truth-lie breaks the twist mechanic. The star is meant to guess, but both lines announce the answer: 'Truth: I've A/B tested my own name. Lie: Dash won.' and 'I've been in a real board meeting. I've never been in love. Second one's the lie. Sorry, first.'
The rhyme twist asks for a couplet. 'Pick me, I'm a rocket, a launch, a sure thing. Pivot: a sure-ish thing. Still rhymes with ring.' is not one; it explains a rhyme it never makes.

The wingman card says 'Not yourself', but 'Brock's honest, strong, proud of you. Pivoting. Have you heard about me?' pitches himself. That is defensible as the joke, but it is the third self-pitch-pivot gag in the bank.
